question: A 9-year-old girl has nasal symptoms on most days of the week for the past 8 months. Her symptoms include nasal blockage and itchy eyes, and they affect her ability to sleep and perform at school. According to the ARIA (Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma) classification, how should her allergic rhinitis be classified?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Intermittent means symptoms occur fewer than 4 days per week OR for fewer than 4 consecutive weeks. This child has symptoms on most days for 8 months, so the duration criterion for 'intermittent' is not met.

The frequency criterion rules out 'intermittent' — symptoms on most days for 8 months classifies as 'persistent'. Even though she has significant impairment, the ARIA duration criterion must be applied first.

She does have persistent symptoms (most days, >4 consecutive weeks), but the severity is not 'mild'. Her symptoms disturb sleep and impair daily activities/school performance — these features define moderate-severe under ARIA.

Correct. ARIA defines 'persistent' as symptoms on ≥4 days per week AND for ≥4 consecutive weeks. 'Moderate-severe' applies when one or more of the following are present: disturbed sleep, impaired daily activities, impaired school performance, or troublesome symptoms. This child meets both criteria.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the ARIA classification: duration axis — intermittent (<4 days/wk OR <4 consecutive weeks) vs persistent (≥4 days/wk AND ≥4 consecutive weeks); severity axis — mild (no impairment) vs moderate-severe (sleep disturbance, impaired daily activities, or troublesome symptoms). Apply both axes systematically.

Well done. Applying the ARIA two-axis classification — duration (intermittent vs persistent) and severity (mild vs moderate-severe) — correctly guides treatment intensity. This child needs a stepwise approach with intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) as the backbone.
